Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: This appeal by the plaintiffs directed against judgment and decree dated 1-2-2012 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur dismissing Title Suit No. 23 of 2008.

2. Plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid suit praying amongst other for the following reliefs:—

“(ক) বাদীপক্ষগন নালিশী খ তফসিলের সম্পত্তি রায়তি স্বত্ত্ব এবং বিকল্প বিরুদ্ধ দখলমূল মালিক মর্ম বিবাদীগন বিরুদ্ধ ঘোষনামূলক ডিক্রী দিত।”

3. The case of plaintiffs is that, suit land originally belongs to Bhawal Raj. The suit land of schedule 'Ka' comprising of an area of 23.13 acres of land recorded in CS khatian No. 7 along with other lands in the name of Kumar Rabindra Narayan Chowdhury settled the suit land in raiyati right. On the death of Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury, his heirs as of tenanted right was owner in possession of the entire land of Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury. As per Court of Wards Act 1879, the management and administration of the property including "Ka" schedule land of CS khatian No.  7 was taken over by the Court of Wards. During the last CS record, it was recorded in the name of Court of Wards, for Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury and others, which was subsequently named as Bhawal Raj Courts of Wards Estate or Bhawal Court of Wards Estate or Court of Wards Bhawal Raj Estate. Bhawal Court of Wards Estate as owner and possessor of `Ka' schedule land with other lands of CS khatian No.  7, settled 'Ka' schedule land with the father and husband of the plaintiff. Bashoruddin and co-sharer, Chand Mia through its own printed pattannama. Basiruddin and Chand Mia became owner and possessor in equal share. While Basiruddin and Chand Mia on the basis of pattannama and dakhila and by paying zamindari taxes to Bhawal Court of Wards Estate, the Government, then province of East Pakistan by giving effect of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act acquired the rent receiving interest of the Zaminder and on taking nominal taxes as land development tax, the tenants were classified as owner of their respective land as per sections 3 and 42 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. After acquisition of the rent receiving interest as aforesaid, Government published final gazette as per provision of section 3 of the aforesaid Act on 24-3-1952. After acquisition of the land as aforesaid, Compensation Assessment Roll were prepared and Zaminder as per the aforesaid compensation assessment roll received compensation and gazette was published on 29-5-1956 as per section 42 of the aforesaid Act by which the Zamindari of Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury of `Ka' schedule land, was acquired and the status of tenant. Basiruddin and Chand Mia were changed and become owners. Accordingly SA khatian was finally published in their names. By opening jote in the revenue office and by paying nominal land development tax possessing the suit land SA khatian No.  63 was finally published in the name of Basiruddin and Chand Mia in equal 8 annas share. Basiruddin and Chand Mia upon an amicable settlement partitioned the kha schedule land by which 'Ka' schedule land fallen in the saham of Basiruddin. After acquisition of the land by the Government, 5.40 acres of land remain in the hand of Basiruddin alone which has been mentioned in 'Kha' schedule. Chand Mia got 'Ga' schedule land which comprising of 0.39 acres of land of dag No. 155/1061, 0.51 acres of land of dag No. 1059, 1.42 acres of land of dag No. 1063, 1.18 acres of land of dag No. 1058, 0.60 acres of land of dag No. 1060, in total, 4.10 acres of land and remaining land, in total 13.36 acres including 12.5 as mentioned in 'Gha' schedule was in ejmlali and co-sharers as owners owned and possessed by cultivation. While the aforesaid land was in possession of co-sharers, 1.48 acres of land was acquired by the Government out of 13.63 acres of land for road and remaining land i.e. 12.15 acres of land, "Gha' schedule, was in ejmali of the co-sharers. While co-sharers as aforesaid was in possession having title there to, Government acquired portion of land for defendant No. 16, the Ministry of Agriculture, defendant No. 17, Rice Research Institution from the land of Chand Mia to the very knowledge of defendant No.  1 and 14 in LA Case No.  100/65-66, recognizing Chand Mia as the owner of the aforesaid land. Compensation was received by Chand Mia while in possession, 12.15 acres of land described in schedule `Gha', constructed homestead, planted trees and cultivated agricultural lands in ejmali, died leaving, defendant No.  6 as heir who along with other co-sharers possessing the land in ejmali. While defendant No. 6, plaintiff and Chand Mia was in possession of the ejmali property of 'Gha' schedule comprising 12.15 acres, Government in LA case No.  5/85-86 acquired 10 acres of land for defendant No.  19, Gazipur District Police Line under defendant No.  18, Ministry of Home Affairs. In LA Case No.  3/2001-2002 Government acquired 0.33 acres of land for defendant No.  26, District Fisheries Officer under defendant No.  25, Ministry of Fisheries and Veterinaries under Government of Bangladesh, in LA Case No.  7/90-91 acquired 0.09 acres of land for defendant No. 20, District Jail, Gazipur under defendant No.  18, Ministry of Home Affairs, in LA Case No.  3/95-96 acquired 0.33 acres of land for Defendant No.  District primary Education office under defendant No. 21 Ministry of Education, Government of Bangladesh, in LA Case No.  5/90-91 acquired .50 acres of land for defendant No.  24, Public Health Engineering Department under defendant No.  23, Ministry of Health, Government of Bangladesh. Government disbursed compensation money part of the afore-said 5 LA cases to the plaintiffs and to the co-sharers having found they are legal title holder. Some greedy person of the locality created obstruction in getting compensation money and gave proposal to defendant No. 6, son of defendant No. 9 and brother of defendant Nos.  1 and 8, but recognized their title over 'Kha' schedule land when they would manage in getting the compensation money to the plaintiffs. Later on, Chand Mia died leaving defendant Nos.  2-5 as heirs. Plaintiffs, the heirs of Chand Mia, defendant Nos. 2-5 are waiting for getting compensation money. 28. Foremost consideration of the appeal as to status of the plaintiff. If the suit land recorded as projabili then plaintiffs have legal protection of law and become malik of the suit land.

29. It is the case of plaintiff that when the land recorded as projabili, Zaminders looses control over this land and tenant become land lord or owner of the land and is protected by law. This dispute as we see reflected in some of the decisions of India and also of our country. In the decision of Sushil Kumar vs. Rajendra Lal, reported in AIR 1954 Calcutta, 413, where it is held that:—

The only point which requires consideration in this appeal is whether the tenancy created in favour of the defendant by Jatindra Nath Bose in the year 1936 is a protected interest under section160(g), Bengal Tenancy Act. This section was enacted to protect a right created with the express permission in writing of the landlord at whose instance the tenure or holding was sold. In order that a lease granted by a defaulting tenant may be a protected interest under this clause, the power to grant it must have been given "expressly and in writing" by his lessor. We have accordingly to consider whether Jatindra Nath Bose was "expressly and in writing" given the power to grant the lease of the description which has been granted in favour of the defendant. The kabuliat executed by the predecessor of Jatindra Nath Bose is Exhibit "A". The relevant recital of this kabuliat is as follows:

"Jamite pushkaradi Khanan o imarat o bagbagicha or ghar chhappar tayyar o nijakarkite kumba projabili kariya pattai hakuke danbikrayadir sattadhikari hayiya putra poutradi warisan krame upasattadhi bhog tapab-shat karite thakibe."

30. It means that the leassee will be entitled to enjoy the usufruct of the land through his sons and grandsons and successors in interest by digging tanks, constructing buildings and raising structures and by exercising rights of gift, sale etc., and by cultivating the land in khas or by establishing tenants. We are informed that the expression "Nijakarkite" 1 which occurs in this kabuliat means khas cultivation, that is, cultivation, by one's own labour. The expression "Projabili" (establishing tenants) has been judicially interpreted by reference to section 160 (g) in some of the decisions of this Court. In the case of Akhil Chandra Mandal vs Ssurendra Nath Dutt, 11 Cal LI 87 (A), the head lease authorized the lessee to raise embankments, bridges, damkhals, cut jungles and "establish tenants according to your desire, construct houses .... And do other acts". Acting under this authority, the leassee created an 'istemrari maurasi mokarari makadami' tenure which is a kind of subordinate tenure and not a raiyati holding. Mr Justice Sarada Charan Mitra who was affirmed on Letters Patent Appeal held:

"The words 'established tenants' do not necessarily indicate that the lessor gave the lessee express authority to create tenancies of the kind set up by the plaintiffs in this case. They are words commonly used in leases to indicate that the tenure created entitled the tenure holder either to cultivate the land himself or cause cultivation by means of tenants."

31. It was accordingly held that the sub-lease was not a protected interest under section 160(g), Bengal Tenancy Act. In our opinion what was decided by Mitra, J in this case was that under the head lease right was conferred upon the lessee to bring in only the cultivating raiyats and as the lessee created a permanent tenure, his act was not an exercise of the power expressly and in writing given to him.

32. The expression "Projabili" as used in this kabuliat was held to include the grant of permanent tenure. With great respect to Mr justice Das, We must observe that he was not quite correct in distinguishing the case of Afazuddi (B) (39 Cal 138) on the ground that what was held to be a protected interest in that case was a non-occupancy right. The facts of that case will show that one Prasanna Kumar Mitra created a permanent tenure in favour of Bhojendra Kumar Sen who in his turn granted a permanent tenure in favour of Bahojendra Kumar Sen who in his turn granted a permanent lease to one Ganesh Chandra Chatterjee and Ganesh Chandra Chatterjee created a raiyati lease in favour of the plaintiff. The tenancy of Bhojendra was sold in execution of a decree for arrears of rent and the purchaser at the rent sale sought to annul the interest of Ganesh and also of the plaintiff. Jenkins CJ and D Chatterjee J held that the interest of Ganesh was protected and therefore the interest of the plaintiff could not be touched.

33. It was clearly held in this case that the permanent tenure in favour of Ganesh was included in the expression "Projabili" which occurred in the head lease and therefore the interest of Ganesh was protected under cl. (g) of section 160, Bengal Tenancy Act, Unfortunately the earlier decision in the case of - "11 Cal LJ 87 (A), was brought to the notice of the learned Judges in 'Afazuddi's case, (B)' with the result that the expression " Projabili" was held to include the creation of a tenure in the latter case, while the decision in the former case was to the contrary. In the case before us, however, the recital in the head lease (Exhibit A) is somewhat different from the recitals in the leases in the two cases discussed above. In this case the expression "projabili" is placed in juxtaposition to the word "Nijakarkite" (cultivation by the lessee himself) and is an alternative to khas cultivation. From a mere reading of the provisions of the two President's Orders quoted earlier it is clear that President's Order No.  69 of 1972 envisages abatement of all kinds of suits or other legal proceedings against the Government of Bangladesh whether or not related to acquisition under the Act when the Government opts not to be a party thereto, while President's Order No.  90 of 1972 seeks abatement only of suits and other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act No.  XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (EB Ordinance No.  III of 1956), or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question. President's Order No.  69 of 1972 covers a much bigger field than President's Order No.  90 of 1972. President's Order No.  69 of 1972 is so to say the genus of which President's Order No.  90 of 1972 is specie. Article 2 of President's Order No.  90 of 1972 begins with the phrase "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". Such a non-obstante clause, it is true, has the effect of abrogating the provisions of prior statute in the event of a conflict between the same and the new statute. But such a non-obstante clause cannot reasonably be read as overriding anything contained in any relevant existing law which is not inconsistent with the new statute. We are unable to see any inconsistency or mutual exclusiveness between the two President's Orders both of which aim at abatement of a suit. As logical sequel the provisions of President's Order No.  69 of 1972 cannot be said to have been abrogated because of the non-obstante clause added to President's Order No.  90 of 1972.

57. In the case of Bangladesh vs Sree Sree Madan Gopal Jew, (1981) 33 DLR (AD) 13, the Appellate Division set at rest all controversy regarding impact of such wholesale acquisition as under:—

"It is to be further observed that it is now well settled on the authority of Jalil Ahmed vs the Province of East Pakistan: (1967) 19 DLR 106 decided by a Special Bench and affirmed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Tanvir Ahmed Siddiki vs the Province of East Pakistan (1968) 20 DLR (SC) 144 PLD 1968 SC 185 that on the publication of the notification under section 3 of the Act, all rent receiving interests including that of Debuttor and Waqf estate stood acquired and all non-retainable khas land also stood vested in the Government." In paragraph 4 of the judgment, it is held: "There is another fact which needs to be noted that in the year 1963 notifications under section 43 of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act have been published acquiring of all interests other than already acquired under section 3 of the Act completing all acquisition proceedings under the Act. All the notifications have been published in the Official Gazette covering all districts of Bangladesh. Another fact that requires to be noted is that President's Order No. 90 of 1972, the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) (Third) Order 1972, was promulgated on 3rd August, 1972 long after the observation made in some of the decisions of the High Court, Dacca on the retention by the Mutwalli or Shebait of an estate on account of non-preparation of the compensation assessment roll. This enactment has been promulgated long after all the acquisition proceedings were completed and long after the observations of the High Court made regarding the non-preparation of the compensation assessment roll. This enactment made in President' Order No.  90 of 1972 clearly states that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act No.  XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1956 (EB Ordinance No III of 1956) or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all order, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders passed in such suit, appeals applications and other legal Proceeding shall cease to have any effect; and no court shall entertain and no person shall bring fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question."
